opus-5.5.text:
Oh, that's a hard one. They're almost opposites as people, and maybe that's what makes it interesting.

Erdős would be the more fun dinner, I think. He was famously social. He'd show up at your door with a suitcase and say "my brain is open," and you'd spend the whole evening on problems. He loved posing questions, especially ones that sound simple but turn out to be very deep. His style was collaborative and playful. Mathematics was a conversation for him, almost a social activity. I'd probably leave with three new problems and a coauthored paper by the end of the week.

Grothendieck is a completely different experience. He wasn't interested in clever tricks or solving one hard problem. He wanted to rebuild the foundations so that the problem would dissolve on its own. He had that image of the rising sea: you don't crack the nut with a hammer, you let the water rise slowly until the shell softens and opens. That way of thinking, finding the right level of generality, the right language, so that hard things become natural, is something I find deeply inspiring. And of course he was a very complicated person. Later in life he withdrew from the mathematical community and wrote these long, intense reflections. So a dinner with him might be less relaxed, but maybe more profound.

If I had to choose, I'd lean toward Grothendieck. Partly because of what I work on now. When you think about AI and mathematics, formalization, building systems that reason, you're asking structural questions: what is the right abstraction, how do you organize mathematical knowledge so that it compounds? That's a very Grothendieckian question. I'd love to ask him what he thinks of machines doing mathematics. Would he see it as a betrayal of the human, contemplative side of math, or as another kind of rising sea?

But honestly, I'd want Erdős at the table too, to keep the mood up. Maybe a dinner for three would be best. Erdős throws out problems, Grothendieck says "that's not the right question," and I just sit there taking notes.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, that's a hard one, because they're almost opposite personalities. Erdős was this wandering, hyper-social collaborator who showed up at your door with a suitcase and said "my brain is open," and Grothendieck was this solitary, almost monastic figure who rebuilt the foundations of geometry and then walked away from everything.

If I'm honest, I think I'd pick Erdős for the dinner. Not because I think his mathematics is deeper than Grothendieck's, I don't, but because dinner is a social act, and Erdős basically lived his life as one long dinner conversation about problems. He'd hand you a conjecture before the appetizers arrived, offer you five hundred dollars for it, and you'd actually leave with something to work on. That's very much how I like to think about math, as something you do with other people, out loud.

Grothendieck I find more fascinating as a human being, and I think his way of seeing is probably closer to what I aspire to, that instinct to find the right level of generality where a problem becomes obvious instead of hard. But I'm not sure I'd get much out of a dinner. He'd either be silent or he'd be talking about ecology and his disillusionment with the institutions, which is interesting, but it's not math. By the end of his life he didn't want visitors at all. So I'd be a little afraid I'd be imposing.

Maybe the real answer is I'd want Erdős for the dinner and Grothendieck for the correspondence. Letters were really his medium. Some of the most important mathematics of the twentieth century happened in his letters to Serre.

I’m not sure that’s something you can explain over dinner, but I’d love to ask.
